sec.title: Background and Objectives:
sec.p: Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) are inflammatory conditions, representing prototype examples of immune-mediated disorders of the peripheral nervous system. Activation of the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB) pathway is crucial for generating immune and inflammatory responses and creating an inflammatory milieu; however, this has not been studied in inflammatory neuropathies. We aimed to quantify the expression levels of two critical genes in the NF-κB pathway (Nfkb1 and Nfkb2), together with a prototype inflammatory gene, Tnfα, in inflammatory neuropathies.

sec.title: Methods:
sec.p: Forty-nine patients with inflammatory neuropathies (GBS = 38, CIDP = 11) were recruited prospectively from a single neurology unit. Gene expression levels of Nfκb1, Nfκb2, and Tnfα were quantified using quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction.

sec.title: Results:
sec.p: There were significantly increased expression levels of Nfκb1 in the inflammatory neuropathy group compared to healthy controls (P = 0.001), GBS versus healthy controls (P = 0.03), and CIDP versus healthy controls (P = 0.003). There were no significant differences in the expression levels of Nfκb2 and Tnfα genes between cases and controls. There was no correlation between the expression levels of these genes and the clinical severity scores.

sec.title: Conclusions:
sec.p: The present study provides evidence for NF-κB pathway activation in inflammatory neuropathies, including both GBS and CIDP, suggesting that this spectrum of disorders may share a common central pathway for immune activation. Thus, the NF-κB pathway plays a critical role in the immunopathogenesis of inflammatory neuropathies; however, the molecular interacting partners within the immune system need to be studied to identify the differential immune trajectories in GBS and CIDP.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Inflammatory neuropathies are a heterogeneous group of immune-mediated disorders of the peripheral nerves. They are defined pathologically by the abnormal infiltration of peripheral nerves, nerve roots, or both by inflammatory cells, followed by demyelination and/or axonal degeneration.[1] Inflammatory neuropathies are classified based on the tempo of clinical progression as acute, subacute, or chronic neuropathies.[2] Inflammation and autoimmunity are central to the pathogenesis of inflammatory neuropathies. Inflammation involves a series of coordinated processes mediated by cytokines, which act as initiators, mediators, and regulators, as well as intracellular signaling molecules and master regulator transcription factors of inflammatory cells. Most studies on inflammation in Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS) and chronic inflammatory demyelinating polyradiculoneuropathy (CIDP) have focused on the cytokines that function as initiators, mediators, and effectors of inflammatory responses. For example, altered levels of such cytokines related to inflammatory T helper (Th) 1 and Th17 have been reported in both GBS,[345] and CIDP.[67]

Besides cytokines, the generation of an inflammatory response depends on the coordinated action of multiple extracellular and intracellular molecules. One of the most critical intracellular molecules of inflammation-related signaling is the nuclear factor-κB (NF-κB). NF-kB serves as the inducible regulator of inflammation. The NF-κB comprises a family of transcription factors involved in the induction of the expression of genes encoding proinflammatory molecules such as cytokines, chemokines, etc.[8] Apart from regulating inflammatory responses, the NF-κB also controls the activation, differentiation, and effector function of inflammatory T cells.[9] Given these functional attributes, the NF-κB appears to be a critical determinant of immune-inflammatory responses.

Abnormal activation of the NF-κB signaling pathway has been reported in several systemic inflammatory conditions, and a dysregulated NF-κB pathway has been implicated in promoting neuroinflammation in neurological disorders, including multiple sclerosis.[81011] However, studies on the role of NF-κB in inflammatory neuropathies are limited. The NF-κB expression was increased in the sciatic nerves of the animal model, experimental allergic neuritis, as well as in the nerve biopsies of patients with GBS, CIDP, and vasculitic neuropathies.[1213] In a recent study, genetic polymorphism in the Nfκb1 gene was significantly associated with GBS.[14]

The NF-κB is a critical transcription factor in the immune cascade leading to the expression of inflammatory markers. Any alterations, whether due to genetic or nongenetic processes, are known to affect the expression and functional attributes of NF-κB. Therefore, examining the role of NF-κB in the inflammatory processes constitutes a crucial step in understanding the pathobiology of inflammatory neuropathies. Hence, the present study was conducted to investigate the role of the NF-κB pathway in the pathobiology of inflammatory neuropathies. This study aimed to explore the role of two critical genes, Nfkb1 and Nfkb2, in patients with inflammatory neuropathies. Additionally, the expression of a prototype inflammatory gene, Tumor necrosis factor alpha (Tnfα), was also examined to understand the impact of NF-κB on the expression of inflammatory genes. The findings were correlated with the clinical and electrophysiological characteristics of these patients.

sec.title: Methods
sec.p: This case-control, hospital-based study was conducted at the National Institute of Mental Health and Neurosciences, Bangalore, India. The study protocol was approved by the Institute Ethics Committee (NIMH/DO/IEC (BS and NS DIV)/2021–22, dated 30th November 2021). Adults (≥18 years) who fulfilled the National Institute of Neurological Disorders and Stroke criteria for GBS[15] or the European Academy of Neurology/Peripheral Nerve Society criteria for CIDP[16] were recruited prospectively from a single neurology unit. Age- and gender-matched healthy volunteers, who were biologically unrelated to the cases, were recruited as controls. Patients who had received plasmapheresis and/or intravenous immunoglobulins during the preceding four weeks were excluded. Additional exclusion criteria for patients and controls were (i) other causes of neuropathy, such as infections (leprosy), hereditary motor and sensory neuropathy, entrapment neuropathies, diabetic distal symmetrical polyneuropathy, trauma, and substance abuse or intake of drugs or toxins, and (ii) medical and neurological conditions that were likely to affect the outcome of immunological test results, such as systemic autoimmune disorders, tuberculosis, and other chronic infections.

Clinical and demographic data, such as age and gender, as well as the details of neurological deficits, including the onset, duration, progression, and clinical severity, were gathered by a face-to-face interview and bedside examination by one of the investigators (MN, SR, PB, AP) in a predesigned proforma [Tables 1 and 2]. Patients of GBS were assessed using the Medical Research Council Sum Score (MRCSS), Hughes disability scale (HDS), Overall disability sum score (ODSS), and the modified Erasmus GBS Outcome Score (mEGOS). Patients with CIDP were assessed using the MRCSS and ODSS. The laboratory data, including electrolytes, cerebrospinal fluid analysis, magnetic resonance (MR) neurography, histological studies, and work-up for secondary causes such as vasculitis and paraneoplastic/paraproteinemic disorders, were reviewed. Electrophysiological testing was performed by one of the investigators (MN, SR, PB, AP). Electrophysiological subtyping in patients with GBS was performed using previously published criteria.[17] A written informed consent was obtained from all the study participants.

sec.p: Peripheral blood samples were collected from all the recruited study participants using aseptic precautions. The peripheral blood mononuclear cells (PBMCs) were separated using the principle of density gradient centrifugation, and the Ficoll-Paque PLUS 1.073 (GE Healthcare Bio-Sciences AB, Sweden) was used. Thereafter, ribonucleic acid (RNA) was extracted using the spin column method with the commercially available QIAamp RNA Blood Mini Kit (Qiagen, Inc., Limburg, The Netherlands). High-quality RNA was reverse-transcribed to complementary deoxyribonucleic acid (cDNA) using the commercially available reverse transcriptase with Ribonuclease H (RNaseH) activity and random hexamer/oligo-dT primers (PrimeScript, Takara Bio).

Quantification of the expression levels of Nfκb1, Nfκb2, and Tnfα genes was carried out using the TaqMan chemistry in a QuantStudio 6 platform (Applied Biosystem, MA 01915, USA). Pre-formulated and designed TaqMan probes spanning exon boundaries to avoid nonspecific amplification were used [Supplementary Table 1]. Amplification of the target genes in each sample was normalized to an endogenous control gene, Tbp. The cycling conditions for the polymerase chain reaction (PCR) were (i) initial denaturation: 95ºC for 20 s, (ii) 95ºC for 1 s for 40 cycles, and (iii) annealing and extension: 60ºC for 20 s. All the reactions were run in triplicate. The cDNA samples were diluted to a final concentration of 10 ng/µl. Quantitative PCR (qPCR) was performed using a commercially available Premix Ex Taq™ (Probe qPCR) 2×master mix (Cat. No. RR390A, Takara). The final reaction mix (10 μl) consisted PCR Master Mix, probes, and cDNA (1 μl). All the amplification batches included a no-template control, and the cDNA of a control subject was used as a calibrator (reference sample). The calibrator was used in each plate to assess the inter-assay variability, which was set at <0.5 Ct. Target and endogenous control gene expression levels were assessed for all samples, and the final results were calculated as a fold-change of target gene expression relative to the reference sample (calibrator), normalized to the endogenous control. The 2-ΔΔCt method of relative quantification (fold-change) was used.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: The data were entered into a pre-designed proforma and incorporated into a Microsoft Excel spreadsheet for analysis. The quantitative data were expressed in mean ± standard deviation or median (interquartile range). The expression levels of the genes in the NF-κB signaling pathway were compared between patients with inflammatory neuropathies and healthy controls using the paired t-test. The gene expression levels were correlated with clinical features, such as severity and electrophysiological subtypes, as well as between the different subgroups of inflammatory neuropathies, including GBS and CIDP, using Spearman’s correlation test. The Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (version 28) was used for analysis of the data. A P value of ≤ 0.05 was considered to be significant.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: The original cohort consisted of 50 patients with inflammatory neuropathies (GBS = 39; CIDP = 11) and an equal number of age- and gender-matched healthy controls (n = 50). However, the gene expression analysis in some study participants (GBS = 1 and healthy controls = 8) did not yield consistent results, even after repeating the experiments three times; therefore, their data had to be excluded from the final analysis. The final cohort comprised 49 patients with inflammatory neuropathies (GBS = 38, CIDP = 11) and 42 controls, who were matched for age and gender as a group. The mean age of cases was 43.67 ± 15.6 years, and there were 30 men and 18 women. The results of gene expression analysis showed a significantly increased expression level of Nfκb1 in the inflammatory neuropathy group compared to the healthy controls (P = 0.001). The gene expression levels of Nfκb1 were significantly higher in the GBS group compared to healthy controls (P = 0.03). The gene expression levels of Nfκb1 were also significantly greater in the CIDP group compared to healthy controls (P = 0.003). There were no significant differences in the gene expression levels of Nfκb2 between inflammatory neuropathies vs healthy controls (P = 0.14), GBS vs healthy controls (P = 0.46), or CIDP vs. healthy controls (P = 0.30). There were no significant differences in the gene expression levels of Tnfα between inflammatory neuropathies vs healthy controls (P = 0.93), GBS vs healthy controls (P = 0.59), or CIDP vs healthy controls (P = 0.28) [Table 3]. Compared to the GBS group, the CIDP group had higher Nfκb1 expression levels (P < 0.001). The Nfκb2 levels were lower in the CIDP compared to the GBS group (P = 0.028). There was no significant difference in the Tnfα expression levels between the GBS and CIDP groups (P = 1.00). Furthermore, there was no correlation between the expression levels of these genes and clinical severity scores, such as MRCSS, HDS, ODSS, and mEGOS, in the GBS group. There was no correlation between the expression levels of these genes and the clinical severity scores, such as MRCSS and ODSS, in the CIDP group [Tables 4 and 5].

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: Immune activation is a consistent pathological basis for inflammatory neuropathies. Inflammation is a complex process, but the central mechanism is the activation of the NF-κB cascade, which is the prototype pathway that signals the generation of proinflammatory responses in the peripheral blood and various tissues in response to exogenous and endogenous triggers. The salient finding of the present study was the significantly upregulated gene expression level of Nfκb1 in the inflammatory neuropathy group as a whole, as well as in the GBS and CIDP groups.

The NF-κB family comprises five structurally related transcription factors, including NF-κB1 (p50), NF-κB2 (p52), RelA (p65), RelB, and c-Rel. These proteins can further be categorized into two groups based on the presence of a transcriptional activation domain. Two members, p50 and p52, do not possess the transcriptional activation domain, while the remaining three, Rel-A, Rel-B, and c-Rel, contain a C-terminal transcriptional activation domain. The p50 and p52 homodimers remain transcriptionally repressive if they are not bound to Rel-A, Rel-B, or c-Rel. The NF-κB transcriptional activity, or signaling, is mediated by canonical and noncanonical pathways.[18] The NF-κB1 is involved in the canonical pathway, while the noncanonical pathway utilizes NF-κB2. The canonical pathway is triggered by diverse stimuli such as pattern recognition receptors, ligands of various cytokine receptors, T and B cell receptors, members of the TNF receptor superfamily, bacterial lipopolysaccharides (LPS), etc., while the noncanonical pathway is selectively stimulated by B-cell activating factor, lymphotoxin-B, CD40 ligand, etc.[19] The NF-κB1 and NF-κB2 have functionally distinct downstream properties. The activation of NF-κB1 induces expression of multiple proinflammatory genes, while NF-κB2 plays a key role in cellular differentiation and development.[20] It is noteworthy that most stimuli of the NF-κB1 pathway have consistently been linked to inflammatory neuropathies.[32122] Furthermore, LPS, which activates NF-κB1, was also isolated from GBS patients.[22] These data provide a strong rationale for Nfkb1 upregulation in patients with inflammatory neuropathies, as noted in the current study. The gene expression levels of Nfκb1 and Nfκb2 exhibited differential expression between GBS and CIDP. A diverse range of environmental and endogenous stimuli activates the NF-κB pathway. Therefore, the precise mechanistic basis of the differential expression of the Nfκb1 and Nfκb2 genes needs to be understood in future studies.

Data on the impact of a dysfunctional NF-κB pathway is limited in peripheral neuropathies, including the inflammatory neuropathies such as GBS and CIDP. Enhanced NF-κB activity was also demonstrated in the peripheral nerves of mice with experimentally induced diabetes and in humans with diabetic neuropathy.[23] Increased expression of NF-κB was demonstrated in the sural nerves of GBS and CIDP compared to noninflammatory neuropathies.[24] In another study, increased expression of the p65 subunit of NF-κB in the blood vessels within the endoneurium, myelin, and axons was demonstrated in CIDP.[13] Thus, the available studies mostly assessed the components of NF-κB signaling in peripheral neuropathies at the tissue level. However, the present study on inflammatory neuropathies assessed the expression level of the NF-κB signaling pathway-related genes in the PBMCs. More recently, we demonstrated significant differences in the single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs) in the promoter region of the Nfκb1 gene in a large cohort of GBS, together with evidence for a combined effect of TLR2 and NFκβ1 SNPs that increased the risk of GBS.[14] In another study, increased levels of certain NF-κB-related transcripts such as ATG5, DICER-AS1, PACER, DILC, NKILA, and ADINR were reported both in GBS and CIDP.[25]

The NF-κB has been correlated with clinical course and disease severity in other systemic inflammatory and immune-mediated demyelinating disorders of the central nervous system.[2627282930] A small cohort study reported increased mRNA expression of NF-κB in the PBMCs of patients with GBS; however, there was no difference between mild and severe GBS.[31] More recently, in an extensive study of 150 patients with GBS, the Nfκb1 genotype did not correlate with the severity, need for mechanical ventilation, or outcome at hospital discharge.[14] In the present study, there was no correlation between the disease severity and the expression levels of the tested genes.

The Nfκb1 gene encodes the p50 subunit, which is the regulatory subunit of NF-κB and plays a crucial role in regulating the process of inflammation. The present study provides evidence for the activation of the NF-κB signalling pathway in inflammatory neuropathies, both in GBS and CIDP, suggesting that this spectrum of disorders may share a common central pathway for immune system activation and the resulting inflammatory response. It is noteworthy that there was no change in the level of expression of the Tnfα gene in both the GBS and CIDP groups compared to healthy controls. NF-κB activation leads to the production of multiple inflammatory cytokines. Therefore, other inflammatory cytokine genes should be examined to understand the impact of elevated NF-κB expression on inflammatory markers. Though a similar expression of the Nfκb1 gene was observed in both GBS and CIDP, the downstream molecular pathways may be unique for GBS and CIDP, and these may govern their respective clinical courses. Thus, the molecular interacting partners of NF-κB within the immune system, particularly its inhibitor, I-κB, need to be explored to explain the differential immune trajectories that underlie GBS and CIDP. Furthermore, the study is limited by its small sample size, particularly in the CIDP group, and requires replication in larger cohorts.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The present study provides evidence for the activation of the NF-κB signalling pathway in inflammatory neuropathies, both in GBS and CIDP, indicating that this spectrum of disorders share a common central pathway for immune system activation and the resulting inflammatory response. The findings of the present study must be confirmed in larger cohorts and patients derived from different populations for further validation. Longitudinal assessment, combined with the simultaneous evaluation of protein levels and genetic polymorphisms, may provide better insights into the role of this pathway in inflammatory neuropathies.
